A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities and countries that work together to deliver websites, videos, and images faster. Without one, every request for a webpage would travel all the way to a single origin server, meaning the main computer where the website's files are originally stored. If that server sits far away, loading takes longer, and heavy traffic can overwhelm it.

A CDN solves this by placing copies of website content on servers positioned closer to people, called edge locations, because they sit at the "edge" of the network, nearest to wherever someone happens to be browsing. When a request arrives, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy of the content. If it does, that outcome is called a cache hit, meaning the answer was already sitting ready and could be sent back immediately, without contacting the original server at all. If not, the edge location fetches the content once from the origin server, stores a copy, and hands it over.

Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books on hand, so readers never need to travel to one central library across the country every time a book is wanted.

This arrangement reduces waiting time, eases pressure on the origin server, and keeps things running smoothly even when many people request the same content at once, which is why so many popular websites rely on this kind of setup behind the scenes.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's files | It's the ultimate source all copies come from |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of content | It shortens the distance data has to travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered from a stored copy | It means faster delivery with less waiting |
| Latency | The delay before content starts loading | Lower delay makes browsing feel smooth and instant |
